title: Sweep and compact
sub: The free list, moving objects and updating references
cards/0/title: Sweep: holes go to the free list
cards/0/body:
If the plan decided to sweep, live objects stay where they are. The GC walks the gaps between plugs:

  • neighboring dead objects merge into one chunk;
  • the chunk is formatted as a free object: a fake object with a special "Free" type and a length;
  • large enough chunks go onto the generation's free list, sorted by size.

Space is later taken from that list: when promoting survivors in the next collection, when allocating in LOH.

The cost of sweep is walking the generation. No copying, no rewriting references. The price of being cheap is fragmentation.
cards/0/deep: Free objects are visible in a dump: !dumpheap -stat in SOS shows a Free row with the count and total size of the chunks. In the .NET 8 sources a chunk smaller than two minimum object sizes (48 bytes on a 64-bit platform) does not go onto the list: it stays a "Free" object, but cannot be used until the next compaction.
cards/1/q: Why format a free chunk as a fake "Free" object instead of leaving the dead objects there?
cards/1/options/0: The heap is walked in order, stepping by object size: the chunk must look like an object with a length, and neighboring dead ones must merge into one
cards/1/options/1: This is how the GC zeroes memory for security
cards/1/options/2: Otherwise the finalizers of dead objects would run again
cards/1/options/3: The free object keeps references to its neighbors for the card table
cards/1/explain: The plan, sweep, the debugger and dumps walk the heap object by object. A free object with type Free and a length keeps the heap walkable, and merging gives one big chunk instead of a scatter of small ones.
cards/2/body:
After a sweep, free memory is scattered in chunks between live objects. An object bigger than the largest chunk will not fit, even if there is plenty free in total. Then the heap needs new memory, and the process grows while the heap is "empty".

This hits LOH especially: by default it is only swept, and the objects there are large.

How much memory sits in chunks is visible from code:
cards/3/q: LOH has 50 free chunks of 1 MB each. The program allocates a 3 MB array. What happens?
cards/3/options/0: No chunk fits: LOH takes new memory even though 50 MB is free
cards/3/options/1: The GC glues three neighboring chunks together and puts the array there
cards/3/options/2: The array is cut into three 1 MB parts
cards/3/explain: An array must be one contiguous piece. The chunks are separated by live objects, and only compaction can join them. Without it LOH grows, and the 50 MB of holes stay holes.
cards/3/wrong/1: If the chunks are separated by live objects, they cannot be joined without moving those objects.
cards/4/body:
If the plan chose compaction, two phases follow.

Relocate: rewrite references. The GC again goes through every place that may hold references into the condemned generations: roots on stacks (using the same GC info), handles, marked cards of older generations, fields of the survivors themselves. For each reference the new address is found through the brick table: find the plug, add its relocation distance.

Compact: copy the plugs to their new places, in address order. Plugs slide toward the start, so copying works like memmove and does not overwrite anything not yet copied.

After that the allocation pointer sits right after the last survivor, and everything beyond it is one solid free area.
cards/5/q: Put the steps of a compacting Gen 0 collection in order
cards/5/items/0: Mark the living from roots and cards
cards/5/items/1: Split into plugs and compute new addresses
cards/5/items/2: Rewrite references to the new addresses
cards/5/items/4: Put the allocation pointer after the last survivor
cards/5/explain: References are rewritten before copying: while objects are still in their old places, the plan in the gaps and the brick table are intact and tell the new addresses.
cards/6/body:
A ref variable, a Span<T>, a reference to an array element point not at the start of an object but into its middle. These are interior pointers.

GC info flags them specially. When it finds one, the GC uses the brick table to find the start of the object it points into, marks that object, and during compaction shifts the pointer by the same distance as the object. That is why a Span over an array needs no pinning.

Finding an object's start from an arbitrary address is not cheap. That is one of the reasons interior pointers live only on the stack: ref fields exist only in a ref struct, and a Span cannot be stored in a class field.
cards/7/q: What will the GC rewrite in the relocate phase if array arr moved? Select all.
cards/7/options/0: The local variable int[] a = arr on the stack
cards/7/options/1: A reference field to arr in a surviving object
cards/7/options/3: The value of arr.GetHashCode() saved in a variable
cards/7/options/4: A long addr into which the address of arr was written earlier via unsafe
cards/7/explain: The GC rewrites what it knows to be references: stack slots from GC info, fields by GCDesc, interior pointers. The hash code does not depend on the address, and a long is just a number to the GC.
cards/8/title: Why moving does not break the hash code
cards/8/body:
If objects move, an address is no good either for a hash or for identity. So the default hash code (RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode) is not an address: on the first call the runtime generates a pseudo-random number and stores it in the object header or in the sync block. The object moves, and the hash moves with it.

But anything you derived from an address yourself lies after compaction. An address from Unsafe.AsPointer without pinning may, one collection later, point at someone else's object or at a free chunk.
cards/8/deep: This ties to the lesson on System.Object in "Deeper C#": the object header is shared by the hash code, the lock bits and the sync block index. If an object needs both a hash and a "fat" lock, the data moves to a sync block, and the header keeps only its index.
cards/9/q: What can happen with this code?
cards/9/options/0: The write may corrupt another object or free memory: arr may have moved
cards/9/options/1: The GC will update p, just as it updates a ref
cards/9/options/3: It will not compile: AsPointer is forbidden for arrays
cards/9/explain: To the GC, a void* is not a reference, and it is not in the GC info. If the collection compacted the generation, p points at the old place of arr, which now holds another object or a free chunk. The bug is silent: memory gets corrupted without an exception.
cards/9/wrong/1: Only places the JIT flagged as references or interior pointers are updated. A void* is not one of them.
cards/10/body:
• Sweep: the cost is proportional to the size of the generation: walk it. Objects do not move, references are not touched. Holes remain.
  • Compact: the cost is proportional to the survivors: copy their bytes and rewrite references to them. No holes, allocation is a pointer bump again, objects keep their relative order and sit tightly (good for the cache).

So for Gen 0, where few survive, compaction is cheap and frequent. Compacting a large Gen 2 is expensive, so it is swept more often (and a background collection only ever sweeps, see "GC modes").

After compaction, emptied regions return to the common pool, and over time the GC gives surplus memory back to the OS (decommit): the very difference between reserve and commit from the first unit.
cards/10/deep: If you care more about memory than CPU, there is the GCConserveMemory setting (values 0 to 9, .NET 6+): the higher the number, the more willingly the GC compacts Gen 2 and LOH to reduce fragmentation. With regions (.NET 7+) survivors can be compacted into other regions too, not only toward the start of the same one, and empty regions go back to the free pool whole.
cards/11/q: Match the phase and its job
cards/11/pairs/1/1: Computes new addresses and picks the cleanup method
cards/11/pairs/2/1: Rewrites references to the new addresses
cards/11/pairs/3/1: Copies plugs to their new places
cards/11/pairs/4/1: Turns holes into the free list
